Prevention: Apply crop rotation with non- solanaceous crops like maize, beans, sunflower etc for at least two years before re-planting with tomato
Use compost, old manure, or rotation with nitrogen-fixing legumes to maintain soil fertility. (Nutrient deficiency increases susceptibility to early blight)
Orient tomato rows to the direction of the wind
Irrigate early in the day to allow drying of leaves
Promote good air circulation in the field by proper spacing (e.g. 60 cm x 30 cm for small varieties, 90 cm x 45 cm for tall varieties)
Solanaceous weeds that may act as hosts
After tomato harvest, bury all plant residues to reduce the spread of the disease to the next season.
Monitoring: Wet weather favours the development of early blight

Inspect the crop twice per week for symptoms of the disease: 0.5 - 3 cm brown irregular spots with sunken rings on leaves and on fruits near fruit stems; The disease starts from the lower, older leaves and moves upwards in the plant.
If 3-5% of plant population have the symptoms, consider action
Direct Control: Hand-pick and remove the diseased foliage outside the field and bury.
Transport the diseased material away from the field in bags to prevent the spread of the disease
Restrictions: Prevention is the most powerful and often only measure; and chemical sprays are often too late or have little effect.

When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre-harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re-entry interval, min retreatment interval.
